title: What Does Website Maintenance Actually Cost?
excerpt: Hosting, security, plugin updates, content changes — website maintenance costs add up in ways that aren't obvious upfront. Here's an honest breakdown for small and medium-sized businesses.

blocks.text: Most businesses know what it costs to build a website. Far fewer know what it costs to keep one running.

'Website maintenance' covers a lot of ground: server costs, security, software updates, performance monitoring, content changes. The total can range from under €20/month to over €400/month depending on your tech stack and what you actually need.
Here's an honest breakdown — what each component costs, where the hidden expenses tend to appear, and how different technology choices affect the total.
What 'Maintenance' Actually Means
Maintenance isn't one thing. It's several recurring cost lines stacked on top of each other.
Hosting

The server or cloud service that makes your site accessible. Cost varies dramatically — from €5/month on shared hosting to €80+/month on managed WordPress hosting. What you pay for is reliability, performance, and how much hand-holding comes included.
Security

SSL certificates, malware scanning, firewall rules, DDoS protection. Not optional. A compromised website damages your reputation, gets you blacklisted by Google, and can expose your customers' data. The cost of cleaning up after a breach is typically far higher than any security subscription.
Software updates

CMS updates, plugin updates, theme updates. Each update needs testing before deployment — a WordPress plugin update can break your layout, your forms, or your checkout. Each skipped update is a potential security vulnerability.
Backups

Daily off-site backups with a tested restore procedure. Often available as an add-on from your host. Worth paying for separately if it's not included — losing a site and rebuilding it from scratch costs far more than any backup plan.
Content changes

Updating copy, adding new pages, swapping images, publishing blog posts. If you're doing this yourself, the cost is your time. If you're paying a developer or agency, it's their hourly or monthly rate.

blocks.text: The range is wide because it depends heavily on how much of this you're handling yourself vs. paying someone to do. A WordPress agency on a monthly retainer typically charges €150–€300/month for basic maintenance: updates, security monitoring, backup management, and minor content changes.
Emergency fixes when something breaks after an update — and it does happen — typically cost an extra €150–€500 on top of whatever you're paying for standard maintenance.
Next.js / Modern Stack Maintenance Costs
A statically-generated Next.js site hosted on Vercel has a fundamentally different cost structure — primarily because the architecture eliminates most of what makes WordPress expensive to maintain.

Security (handled at edge by Vercel, no plugin needed)

blocks.text: The main savings come from eliminating ongoing security plugin fees and drastically reducing update frequency. WordPress plus an average plugin set can require attention weekly. Next.js gets a major release roughly once a year.

That said, when a Next.js site does need updates, you'll want a developer — unlike WordPress, you can't click 'Update' in an admin panel. The tradeoff is lower frequency in exchange for requiring technical skill when it does arise.
The Hidden Cost: Developer Dependency

On a typical WordPress site, many content changes require someone with WordPress access — and often a developer if the change touches the theme or layout. A 15-minute text update can become a 2-hour task if something breaks during a plugin update that happened to coincide.

On a well-built Next.js site with a headless CMS, non-technical team members can manage content independently. If your business changes prices, adds services, or publishes content regularly, the time saved over a year adds up to a real cost difference.
What's Worth Paying For
Not all maintenance spending is equal. These are the line items that actually protect your business:

items: **Managed hosting with automatic backups** — losing a site and rebuilding it from scratch costs far more than any hosting plan. Don't cut corners here.
**Security monitoring with alerting** — catching a breach within hours limits the damage; finding out weeks later does not.
**A developer relationship before you need it** — having someone who knows your site when something breaks is worth the cost of maintaining contact even in quiet months.
**Performance monitoring** — Google's Core Web Vitals affect rankings. A site that degrades slowly over time loses traffic slowly over time.

blocks.text: Red Flags in Maintenance Contracts

items: **'Unlimited changes' at a flat rate** — read the small print. 'Change' usually means minor text edits, not new pages, layout work, or feature additions.
**No defined SLA on response times** — a vague promise of 'prompt response' isn't useful when your site is down on a Monday morning.
**No backup policy in writing** — if they can't tell you how often backups run, where they're stored, and how long a restore takes, they may not be doing it.
**12-month lock-in without exit terms** — a competent provider doesn't need to trap you. Exit conditions should be clear from the start.
